Viticulture

Vine diseases and pests: powdery mildew, downy mildew, botrytis and more

An overview of the main fungi, bacteria, viruses and insects that threaten the vineyard, how to recognise them and how they are controlled today.

The European vine, Vitis vinifera, is a sensitive plant. For thousands of years it lived alongside few serious enemies, but in the nineteenth century growing trade brought from America several organisms against which it had no defences. Since then, plant protection has been one of the grower's central tasks, and the decisions taken affect both the quantity of grapes and the quality of the wine.

Powdery mildew

Powdery mildew, also known as oidium, is caused by the fungus Erysiphe necator, which arrived in Europe from America in the mid-nineteenth century. It shows up as a greyish-white powder on leaves, shoots and bunches, with a typical mouldy smell. On young berries it stops the skin from growing, so the skin splits while the pulp keeps expanding; split grapes dry out or rot. Unlike other fungi, powdery mildew does not need rain: it thrives in mild, overcast and slightly humid weather.

The historic remedy, still fundamental today, is sulphur, applied as a dust or as a spray. Modern fungicides are added to it, along with practices such as summer pruning and leaf removal, which open up the canopy and reduce the conditions the fungus favours.

Downy mildew

Downy mildew, caused by Plasmopara viticola, also of American origin, reached France a few decades after powdery mildew. It is closely tied to water: it needs rain and mild temperatures to infect. Yellowish, translucent patches known as “oil spots” appear on the upper side of the leaf, with a white down on the underside. If it attacks young bunches, it dries them out or turns them brown and shrivelled. In wet years it can destroy a large part of the crop.

To fight it, Bordeaux mixture was developed: a blend of copper sulphate and lime devised in Bordeaux at the end of the nineteenth century, which marked the beginning of chemical vine protection. Copper remains an essential tool, above all in organic viticulture, although its build-up in the soil has led to limits on the permitted doses.

Botrytis: grey rot and noble rot

Botrytis cinerea is a fungus with two faces. When humidity persists close to harvest it causes grey rot: the berries become covered in a grey mould, burst, and give the wine mouldy and oxidised aromas as well as colour problems. Compact bunches and wounds caused by insects or hail encourage its spread.

However, when damp, misty mornings are followed by sunny, dry afternoons, the same fungus can develop in a controlled way on healthy, ripe grapes. It pierces the skin, the berry loses water and its sugars and acids become concentrated. This is noble rot, the basis of great sweet wines such as those of Sauternes or Tokaji Aszú. The difference between the two forms depends almost entirely on the autumn weather.

Other fungal diseases

  • Black rot: another American disease, it mummifies the berries, which turn black and hard. It is more common in warm, humid areas.
  • Phomopsis (excoriose): it attacks the base of the shoots and can weaken the vine over the years.
  • Grapevine trunk diseases: a group of disorders caused by several fungi that enter through pruning wounds and colonise the trunk. The best known is esca, which can cause a vine to wilt suddenly in midsummer. No fully effective cure exists, so prevention —careful pruning and protecting the cuts— is essential. Their spread is a concern in many regions of the world.

Bacteria, viruses and phytoplasmas

Pierce's disease, caused by the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa and transmitted by sap-feeding insects, blocks the plant's vessels and can kill it. It is a serious problem in parts of the Americas, and its presence in Europe calls for strict surveillance.

Viruses, such as fanleaf or the leafroll viruses, spread mainly through infected planting material and, in some cases, through nematodes or mealybugs. They reduce vigour, delay ripening and lower quality. They cannot be cured in the vineyard, hence the importance of planting healthy, certified material.

Flavescence dorée, caused by a phytoplasma and spread by a leafhopper, is a quarantine disease in Europe: affected vines must be uprooted, and treatments against the insect vector are compulsory in designated areas.

Animal pests

Besides phylloxera, now controlled thanks to rootstocks, vineyards suffer from other pests. The European grapevine moth (Lobesia botrana) is one of the most widespread in Europe: its larvae bore into the berries and open the way to botrytis. Mites, leafhoppers, mealybugs and thrips can also cause damage, as can birds, wild boar and other animals that feed on ripe grapes.

How vineyards are protected today

Modern viticulture tends towards integrated management, which combines several methods to reduce the use of plant protection products:

  • Cultural prevention: choice of site, row orientation, planting density, canopy management and leaf removal to improve airflow.
  • Forecasting models: weather stations and risk models that indicate when an infection is likely, so that vines are treated only when necessary.
  • Biological control: beneficial fauna that prey on pests, and techniques such as mating disruption, which releases pheromones to prevent male moths from finding females.
  • Resistant varieties: new varieties obtained by crossing, sometimes called PIWI, which combine genes for resistance to downy and powdery mildew with a profile close to that of vinifera.

Organic viticulture relies mainly on sulphur, copper and natural extracts. Climate change, with more erratic springs and new pests moving northwards, is altering the timing and intensity of many of these problems, and is forcing growers to watch their vines ever more closely.
